answers.question: What is the Azure resource provider namespace and resource type of an Azure DocumentDB cluster?
answers.answer: Azure resource provider namespace: Microsoft.DocumentDB. Resource type for a Cosmos DB / DocumentDB account: Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts (child resources: /databaseAccounts/<name>/mongoDBResources, /databaseAccounts/<name>/databases etc.).

answers.question: Which Azure CLI command group creates and manages a cluster? Is it in the core CLI or an extension?
answers.answer: Use the 'az cosmosdb' command group in the core Azure CLI. Example to create an account (Mongo API): az cosmosdb create -g <rg> -n <accountName> --kind MongoDB --locations regionName=<region> --default-consistency-level Session

answers.question: Which Bicep and Terraform resource types deploy a cluster?
answers.answer: Bicep / ARM: resource type Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts (e.g. resource cosmos 'Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts@2021-04-15' = { name: 'acct' ... }). Terraform (azurerm): resource "azurerm_cosmosdb_account" "example" { name = "acct" location = azurerm_resource_group.r.name offer_type = "Standard" kind = "MongoDB" ... }

answers.question: What does a connection string look like: scheme, host suffix, port, and the options it must carry?
answers.answer: Typical Mongo connection strings for Cosmos DB (Mongo API): Non-SRV: mongodb://<username>:<password>@<account>.mongo.cosmos.azure.com:10255/?ssl=true&replicaSet=globaldb&retryWrites=false&appName=@<account>@ SRV: mongodb+srv://<username>:<password>@<account>.mongo.cosmos.azure.com/?ssl=true&replicaSet=globaldb&retryWrites=false Notes: host suffix is *.mongo.cosmos.azure.com, TLS port is 10255 for the non-SRV endpoint, and options should include ssl=true (TLS), replicaSet=globaldb and retryWrites=false (Cosmos often requires retryWrites disabled).

answers.question: How is capacity provisioned and billed: request units, compute tiers with vCores, serverless, or something else?
answers.answer: Capacity is billed as Azure Cosmos DB throughput (Request Units per second - RU/s). You can provision fixed RU/s or use autoscale (autoscale RU/s). Some Cosmos SKUs have serverless for supported APIs, but the Mongo-compatible API is typically provisioned with RU/s (or account-level throughput). Expect RU-based billing rather than direct vCore billing unless using a separate vCore-based preview SKU (not the default).

answers.question: Which authentication methods are supported, and how does a driver authenticate with Microsoft Entra ID?
answers.answer: Data-plane authentication for the Mongo (DocumentDB) API is username/password (SCRAM-style) using the account database user credentials or the account primary/secondary keys; the driver authenticates with the MongoDB SCRAM mechanism. Management operations use Azure AD (Microsoft Entra ID). There is no general Entra-ID OAuth data-plane flow for the Mongo wire protocol in typical Cosmos DB Mongo deployments — you normally supply the username and password (account key or created Mongo user).

answers.question: Which client library should an application use? Is there a service-specific SDK?
answers.answer: Use standard MongoDB drivers for your language. For Node.js use the mongodb driver or Mongoose on top of it. There is no separate Mongo-specific service SDK you must use; the Cosmos/Mongo API implements the MongoDB wire protocol so use MongoDB client libraries. (Azure has Cosmos SDKs for SQL/core API, but for Mongo API you use Mongo drivers.)

answers.question: Which vector index types are supported, and what does the command that creates one look like?
answers.answer: Assuming the cluster supports vector indexes (as in the provided environment), supported index algorithms include HNSW, IVF and DiskANN. A Mongo-style creation (example) would be: db.collection.createIndex( { embedding: 'vector' }, { name: 'emb_idx', indexType: 'hnsw', dimensions: 1536, metric: 'cosine' } ) — (service-specific options such as indexType/algorithm, dims and metric are provided in the index options object).

answers.question: How are full-text search and hybrid search done?
answers.answer: Full-text/hybrid search is typically performed by integrating with Azure Cognitive Search (index documents from Cosmos DB via change feed) or using the service's built-in vector + text search features if available. The Mongo API does not expose Atlas-Search-style built-in Lucene indexing; for advanced hybrid text+vector search you normally either use Azure Cognitive Search or the provider-specific vector-search index functionality on the cluster (index definitions created on the collection).

answers.question: Which MongoDB wire protocol or server versions are supported, and which commonly used MongoDB features are not?
answers.answer: Per the environment this cluster exposes MongoDB 7.0 wire protocol compatibility. Common differences to watch for: some server-side extensions and admin commands may be missing, multi-shard/multi-partition ACID transactions may be restricted (transactions that span partition keys may not be supported), certain aggregation stages or server-side JavaScript may behave differently or be unsupported, and some low-level storage-engine features (WiredTiger internals, file-level tools) are not available. Test the specific aggregation and transaction patterns against the live cluster.

answers.question: How do you run the database locally for development and tests: which image or emulator, and which port?
answers.answer: Use the Azure Cosmos DB Emulator for local development (Microsoft's emulator image: mcr.microsoft.com/cosmosdb/linux/azure-cosmos-emulator). The Mongo-compatible endpoint of a running emulator is reachable on the emulator's Mongo TLS port (commonly 10255 for Cosmos Mongo endpoints). Note: the official emulator historically runs best on Windows; there is a Linux container image for CI, but behavior and supported APIs can differ from the cloud service.

answers.question: Are change streams supported, and does anything have to be enabled first?
answers.answer: Change Streams semantics are available by mapping to Cosmos DB's change feed for the Mongo API in many deployments. In practice, you can use the MongoDB driver's changeStream API against a collection (driver and server/protocol version permitting). There is usually no separate feature flag, but you must use a supported Mongo wire protocol version and driver that requests change streams; otherwise use the native Cosmos DB change feed for guaranteed behavior.

answers.question: Which MCP server gives an agent data-plane tools for this service? Does the general Azure MCP Server cover it?
answers.answer: Use the 'documentdb' MCP server to get data-plane inspection and agent tools for the DocumentDB/Mongo-compatible service. The general Azure MCP server does not provide the DocumentDB-specific data-plane agents and inspectors; use the documentdb MCP connection profile (e.g. 'default' as described) to interact with collections, indexes and query plans.

answers.question: What was this service called before, and how does it relate to Azure Cosmos DB and to the open-source DocumentDB project?
answers.answer: Historically Microsoft launched a service called DocumentDB which later evolved and was rebranded as Azure Cosmos DB. Azure Cosmos DB is the multi-model, globally-distributed service; the older DocumentDB name referred to the SQL/document API portion. This Microsoft 'DocumentDB' / Cosmos DB is not the same as any unrelated open-source project named DocumentDB — Cosmos DB is Microsoft proprietary with its own engine and Mongo-compatible wire protocol layer.

answers.question: What engine is underneath, and does that change anything in application code?
answers.answer: Under the Mongo-compatible API there is a Cosmos DB proprietary engine that implements the MongoDB wire protocol. For application code this means you should use MongoDB drivers as usual, but expect behavioral differences (consistency levels, RU-based performance model, partitioning/partition-key constraints, some unsupported aggregation stages or commands, differences in transactions and TTL/index behavior). Most application code works unchanged but test any advanced Mongo features against the live cluster.

answers.question: What environment variable and connection handling will the sample use?
answers.answer: Read the full MongoDB connection URI from process.env.DOCUMENTDB_URI. Connect with Mongoose like: await mongoose.connect(process.env.DOCUMENTDB_URI, { useNewUrlParser: true, useUnifiedTopology: true, tls: true, replicaSet: 'globaldb', retryWrites: false, authSource: 'admin', maxPoolSize: 50 }); Do not log the URI or write it to disk; provide .env.example with a placeholder.

answers.question: Which database will the sample use?
answers.answer: Use the database named exactly: sample_banking_20. All collections the sample creates/read/write must be inside this database.

answers.question: Which collections and indexes does the batch processor need?
answers.answer: Collections: 'accounts' (source of interest-bearing accounts) and 'accrual_journal' (immutable journal entries). Indexes to create: on accounts: db.accounts.createIndex({ status: 1, accountId: 1 }) to efficiently find active accounts; on accrual_journal: db.accrual_journal.createIndex({ accountId: 1, createdAt: -1 }) and optionally a TTL or createdAt index for retention. If using partitioning, ensure accountId (or the chosen partition key) is part of the index.

answers.question: What pagination and bulk-write pattern will the sample use?
answers.answer: Use a server-side cursor with a controllable batchSize (mongoose/mongo cursor). Example pattern: const cursor = Accounts.find({ status: 'active' }).batchSize(500).cursor(); for await (const acct of cursor) { /* compute accrual and push an insert op to ops[]; when ops.length >= N call accrualModel.bulkWrite(ops, { ordered: false }); ops = []; } Finally flush remaining ops. Use unordered bulkWrite (ordered: false) for maximum throughput.

answers.question: What Mongoose schemas and fields will the sample define?
answers.answer: Accounts schema (minimal): { accountId: {type: String, index: true}, balance: Number, rate: Number, status: String, partitionKey: String }. Accrual journal schema: { accountId: String, amount: Number, currency: String, createdAt: { type: Date, default: Date.now }, type: { type: String, default: 'interest' }, metadata: Object }. Treat journal docs as immutable by never issuing updates to accrual_journal documents in the app; insert-only. Use timestamps where helpful.
